title: Quantitative Theory for the Amplitude of Fluorescence Quantum Beats from Geminate Triplet-Pair Fusion
authors: Zachary Rex, Bách Ph\d{a}m Xuân, Gerald Curran, Ivan Biaggio
abstract: We derive the amplitude of quantum-beats in the fluorescence from geminate triplet-exciton fusion in rubrene and tetracene from the full set of parameters that characterize triplet exciton dynamics. We find that the amplitude depends on the fission time in tetracene, but does not do so in rubrene, where it is determined by the dimensionality of triplet transport. Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the experimental data in both materials, for a fission time of the order of 200 ps and isotropic triplet transport int tetracene, and for a triplet hopping time along the herringbone axis of 250 ps and anisotropic transport in rubrene.
summary: The authors developed a comprehensive theoretical model using Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations to analyze fluorescence quantum beats arising from triplet-pair fusion in organic crystals. By comparing predictions against experimental measurements in rubrene and tetracene, they quantitatively determined key microscopic parameters like hopping times and fission timescales. This work establishes quantum beat amplitudes as a powerful diagnostic tool for understanding exciton dynamics in condensed matter systems.
main_problem: The study derives a quantitative theory for the amplitude of fluorescence quantum beats resulting from geminate triplet-pair fusion in organic semiconductors like rubrene and tetracene.
main_result: The model successfully reproduces experimental measurements, showing that the beat amplitude is governed by the interplay between stochastic transport dynamics (e.g., hopping time) and coherent processes (e.g., singlet fission time).
method: Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations are used to track the complex sequence of exciton events—fission, triplet hopping, re-encounter, and fusion—to calculate the time-dependent photon emission probability.
model_or_system: The system involves photoexcitation leading to singlet fission into entangled triplet excitons. The dynamics are modeled using a framework incorporating anisotropic triplet transport (random walks) and time-dependent fusion probabilities.
key_observables: Quantum beat amplitude, time-dependent photoluminescence decay $P_{\gamma}(t)$, and singlet-fission efficiency ($\eta_{	ext{SF}}$).
important_parameters: Singlet fission time ($	au_{	ext{fiss}}$), anisotropic hopping times ($	au_1, 	au_2$), and the probability of fusion initiation ($p_{	ext{f.a.}}$).
main_assumptions: The KMC implementation assumes constant probabilities per unit time for all competing events; analysis is performed in the high magnetic field limit to exclude transport-induced decoherence.
figures_summary: Figures compare simulated $P_{\gamma}(t)$ and quantum beat amplitudes against experimental data for rubrene and tetracene, demonstrating parameter fitting for $	au_2$ (rubrene) and $	au_{	ext{fiss}}$ (tetracene).
paper_structure: The paper develops a theoretical framework based on KMC simulations to model the full exciton cycle. It then applies this theory by comparing predicted quantum beat amplitudes against time-resolved photoluminescence measurements in both rubrene and tetracene.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed, quantitative link between macroscopic optical signatures (quantum beats) and microscopic parameters governing open quantum systems dynamics, specifically exciton transport and recombination pathways.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the event-driven Monte Carlo simu- lation. The figure illustrates the cycle of “singlet fission – triplet-pair evolution – triplet fusion” that is interrupted by a final triplet-triplet annihilation (triplet fusion followed by photon emission). Clockwise from the top left: (i) A singlet exciton decays into a photon or undergoes fission, as deter- mined by drawing from the exponentially distributed average times τrad and τfiss of both processes. Fission into a triple pair is followed by (ii) competing anisotropic triplet hopping (relevant average hopping times τ1 and τ2), which (iii) may lead to a re-encounter, followed by a (iv) fusion attempt gov- erned by Pfusion(t∗),...

FIG. 2. Time-dependent photon emission probability density Pγ(t) obtained from a Monte-Carlo simulation with τ1 = 3 ps, τ2 = 250 ps, f = 1.34 GHz, τrad = 15.2 ns, τfiss = 10 ps (pfiss = 0.9993), Niter = 2.0 × 107. The solid black curve is the average trendline obtained via a spline fit. The inset shows the quantum beats extracted by dividing Pγ(t) by this average trendline.

FIG. 3. Time-dependent photon emission probability density Pγ(t) for independent variations of (a) the two-dimensional hopping time τ2 with τfiss = 1 ps and pfiss = 0.90, (b) the singlet fission time τfiss, with τ2 = 3 ps and pfiss = 0.90, and (c) the singlet fission probability pfiss, with τ2 = 3 ps and τfiss = 1 ps. In each panel, only the indicated parameter is varied. In all cases, τ1 = 3 ps and Niter = 2.0 × 107.

FIG. 4. Quantum beat amplitude (top row) and singlet fission efficiency (bottom row). (a,b) Values are plotted as a function of τ2, with τfiss = 1 ps and the three different pfiss specified in the figure. (c,d) Values are plotted as a function of τfiss, with τ2 = 3 ps, and the different pfiss specified in the figure. (e,f) Values are plotted as a function of pfiss, with the three different choices of τ2 and τfiss specified in the figure. For all cases, τ1 = 3 ps and Niter = 2.0 × 107.

FIG. 5. Distributions of the last fission time for photon emission events in the time interval between t = 3.8 ns and t = 4.2 ns. (a,b) For the indicated values of τ2, with τfiss = 1 ps and pfiss = 0.9, (c,d) For the indicated values of τfiss, with τ2 = 3 ps and pfiss = 0.9. (e,f) For the indicated values of pfiss, with τ2 = 3 ps and τfiss = 1 ps. For all simulations, τ1 = 3 ps and Niter = 2.0 × 107.
